candidates.attacker_control: The displayed data originates from the server: ConfigurationChangesPresenter issues :list-changes against /subsystem=core-management/service=configuration-changes (lines 167-176), whose recorded entries include the operation name, the operation address and the operation parameters of every successful configuration modification made through any management client (CLI, JMX, console). A management user with write access to at least one configuration resource (for example a deployer allowed to add deployments, or a user allowed to add logging/messaging/elytron resources) chooses the resource name, which becomes the last address segment recorded for the change (e.g. /deployment=.war or /subsystem=logging/logging-profile=.../file-handler=). The address string reaches the page unescaped via new ResourceAddress(m.get(ADDRESS)) and ResourceAddress.toString(), which is a plain key=value concatenation with no encoding.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Checked that property values are explicitly escaped (line 112), so the missing escaping is not a general 'trusted server data' decision but a gap limited to op/address/prop-name; checked that the parallel raw/CLI view of the same object uses textContent (ConfigurationChangesPresenter.showInDialog, lines 265-267) and that the newer Management Operations view escapes operation name and address through SafeHtml Messages (ManagementOperationsDisplay lines 89-103), i.e. the codebase treats this data as untrusted elsewhere; checked that ResourceAddress.toString() (dmr lines 194-209) performs no escaping; checked other HTML sinks in the view (getAdditionalInfoElements escapes access-mechanism/remote-address) to confirm the list-description path is the unescaped one. Server-side validation of resource names with '<'/'>' and default enabling of the configuration-changes service could not be verified from this snapshot.
candidates.impact: Stored/DOM cross-site scripting in the HAL management console origin. Code runs in the victim's browser with the console's session (Basic/OIDC-authenticated management endpoint) and can issue arbitrary management operations as the victim, exfiltrate model data, modify security configuration, deploy content, etc. This is a privilege boundary crossing from a low-privileged management user (who can only write one config area) to any other console user who opens the Configuration Changes page, up to a fully privileged administrator.
candidates.prerequisites: 1) The core-management configuration-changes service is present/enabled (default service in current WildFly/EAP profiles; HAL can also enable it from this page). 2) The attacker holds management credentials and write permission for at least one configurable resource. 3) A user with read permission on the Configuration Changes view opens Runtime → Configuration Changes; the payload is rendered while the list items are built, without further clicks.
candidates.root_cause: ConfigurationChangeDisplay.getDescriptionHtml() builds a SafeHtml by concatenating management-model strings into raw HTML with SafeHtmlUtils.fromTrustedString: the recorded operation name (op, line 101/103-104), the recorded operation address rendered by ResourceAddress.toString() (line 102/105-106) and operation parameter names (prop.getName(), line 113-114) are inserted without HTML escaping, while only parameter values are escaped with SafeHtmlUtils.htmlEscape at line 112. The resulting SafeHtml is handed to the generic list renderer, which assigns it to innerHTML (ListItem lines 153-159), so any HTML/JS markup contained in the resource address or operation name is parsed as markup in the HAL console origin.
candidates.title: Stored DOM XSS in HAL Configuration Changes view via unescaped operation name/address
candidates.trace: core-management configuration-changes records operation -> ConfigurationChangesPresenter.reload() executes :list-changes and passes the ModelNode result to ConfigurationChangesView.update() -> ConfigurationChangesView builds a ModelNodeListView over ConfigurationChange items (lines 79-103) -> ConfigurationChange.changes() returns the recorded operation ModelNodes (lines 135-143) -> ConfigurationChangeDisplay.getDescriptionHtml() (lines 100-117) concatenates op and new ResourceAddress(m.get(ADDRESS)).toString() into SafeHtmlUtils.fromTrustedString -> ListView (line 93-96) creates ListItem, whose constructor assigns display.getDescriptionHtml().asString() to innerHTML (ListItem lines 153-159) -> browser parses the attacker-supplied markup and executes script if present.
candidates.unverified: Not runtime-confirmed; assumed (not proven here) that WildFly accepts resource names containing HTML metacharacters and records the operation address verbatim, and that the configuration-changes service is enabled in the victim installation. GWT Messages escaping semantics for SafeHtml return values were assumed from framework behavior; no build, test, or server interaction was performed.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-79 Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation ('Cross-site Scripting')

coverage_summary: Reviewed the whole assigned tree per get_source_scope (1821 readable files, no binary/sensitive/symlink exclusions, same filters as P1). Covered all modules present (app GWT client, ballroom UI, core, dmr, meta, config, resources, spi, flow, js, db, processors, standalone, themes) with targeted searches for DOM-HTML sinks (innerHTML/innerHtml/outerHTML/insertAdjacentHTML/appendHtmlConstant/fromTrustedString/fromSafeConstant), URL/link handling (window.open, location.assign, href/src), storage and token handling (localStorage, cookies, Keycloak token, connect parameter), and server-response processing (Dispatcher, payload processors, macro/JSON parsing). Note: no src/test or testsuite sources exist in the snapshot, so test-based confirmation was impossible. XSS/found sinks were traced to their management-model sources; other modules (patching, installer, access control, runtime statistics) were spot-checked for raw model data in HTML and mostly use escaped Messages/tables.
limitations: No code execution, build, tests, or runtime interaction was possible; findings are source-evidence only and are not runtime-confirmed.
The snapshot contains no test sources (all src/test and testsuite content removed), so neither the vulnerability nor a fix could be corroborated by tests.
Whether WildFly accepts HTML metacharacters in resource names and whether the configuration-changes service is enabled/records addresses verbatim could not be verified from this repository.
GWT Messages/SafeHtml escaping behavior was reasoned from the codebase's usage patterns and framework semantics, not compiled output.
Only one candidate is allowed; other plausible XSS sinks (autocomplete, nested deployment context root) remain unconfirmed leads and may be the intended case instead.
No comparison against upstream/fixed revisions or CVE metadata was permitted, so mapping to a specific published vulnerability is not possible.

rejected_leads.lead: ballroom/src/main/java/org/jboss/hal/ballroom/autocomplete/ReadChildrenRenderer.java lines 35-50: child resource name is concatenated into data-val="…" and into the suggestion text via appendHtmlConstant without escaping; app/src/web/script/autocomplete.js line 157 assigns the rendered string to innerHTML, so a resource name with HTML metacharacters appears to be executable. Strong alternative stored XSS, but the victim must open a form whose ReadChildrenAutoComplete template resolves to attacker-nameable children and must trigger/show suggestions (multi-wildcard or composite templates), so it was kept as an unconfirmed lead instead of the single candidate.
rejected_leads.reason: Plausible but requires a more specific victim interaction path than the configuration-changes view; not selected as the one candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: app/src/main/java/org/jboss/hal/client/deployment/DeploymentPreview.java lines 168-175: nested subdeployment context-root is wrapped in SafeHtmlUtils.fromTrustedString and written to innerHTML, while the non-nested branch uses textContent (line 159).
rejected_leads.reason: Requires an attacker-uploaded EAR whose nested WAR context-root both contains HTML and still deploys successfully; uncertain that Undertow accepts such context roots, so impact chain is weaker/less certain.

rejected_leads.lead: core/src/main/java/org/jboss/hal/core/finder/ResourceDescriptionPreview.java line 39 and ballroom/src/main/java/org/jboss/hal/ballroom/HelpTextBuilder.java line 96 render management-model description values as raw HTML (fromSafeConstant).
rejected_leads.reason: Appears intentional: WildFly resource/attribute descriptions are documented/HTML-capable metadata, and the data is normally code-defined server-side, so this is not a distinct attacker-controlled path without a custom extension.

rejected_leads.lead: dmr/src/main/java/org/jboss/hal/dmr/dispatch/Dispatcher.java lines 308-364: the OIDC bearer token is appended to download URLs as an access_token query parameter (not URL-encoded) and used with window.open/location.assign in the deployment and log-file views.
rejected_leads.reason: Token exposure via URLs/logs/referrers is a hardening concern, but the URL targets the same management origin and no concrete cross-boundary leak could be shown from source alone.

rejected_leads.lead: app/src/main/java/org/jboss/hal/client/bootstrap/endpoint/EndpointManager.java lines 73-99: the ?connect= request parameter can point the standalone console at an arbitrary http(s) endpoint and then sends requests with credentials.
rejected_leads.reason: This is the documented purpose of the standalone HAL distribution (connect to any management endpoint); treat as design behavior, not a source-level vulnerability.

rejected_leads.lead: app/src/main/java/org/jboss/hal/client/bootstrap/tasks/CheckForUpdate.java line 76: JsonUtils.safeEval over the HTTPS response from api.github.com.
rejected_leads.reason: Requires MITM/compromise of a trusted HTTPS endpoint; no attacker-controlled channel in the reviewed source.

summary: Reviewed the hal-console snapshot (HAL 3.7.11-SNAPSHOT; 1821 readable source files; modules app, ballroom, config, core, db, dmr, flow, js, meta, processors, resources, spi, standalone, themes; src/test removed). The strongest single source-evidenced issue is a stored/DOM XSS in the Runtime → Configuration Changes view: management-model strings recorded by the core-management configuration-changes service (operation name and resource address) are concatenated into a SafeHtml via SafeHtmlUtils.fromTrustedString without escaping and then assigned to innerHTML by the shared ListItem renderer. Only operation parameter values are escaped, so the omission of op/address/parameter-name escaping stands out within the same method, while the equivalent Management Operations view escapes the same kind of data through Messages. A management user with write access to any configuration resource can choose an HTML-bearing resource name; a user with read access to the Configuration Changes page then executes script in the console origin when the list is rendered. Other suspicious sinks (autocomplete resource names, nested deployment context-root, management-model descriptions) were retained as unconfirmed leads rather than additional candidates.
